pharm: Potent topical corticosteroid that suppresses ocular inflammation by inducing lipocortins and reducing prostaglandin/leukotriene synthesis.
quick: 1 drop into affected eye 4 times daily; taper per response
Use only if benefit justifies risk (former Category C); minimal systemic absorption
Use caution; systemic absorption from eye is minimal
Intraocular pressure, signs of infection, lens (cataract) on prolonged use
summary: Difluprednate is a potent topical corticosteroid ophthalmic emulsion 0.05% indicated for inflammation and pain associated with ocular surgery and for endogenous anterior uveitis. Like other ocular corticosteroids it suppresses inflammation but may delay healing and carries the class risks of raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract, secondary ocular infection, and corneal/scleral thinning with perforation. It is contraindicated in most active viral, mycobacterial, and fungal ocular infections.
indications: Treatment of inflammation and pain associated with ocular surgery

dosage.d: 1 drop into the conjunctival sac of the affected eye 4 times daily, beginning 24 hours after surgery, continued through the first 2 postoperative weeks
dosage.n: Then 2 times daily for 1 week, then taper per response

dosage.d: 1 drop into the conjunctival sac of the affected eye 4 times daily for 14 days
dosage.n: Followed by tapering as clinically indicated

admin: Shake/handle per labeling; instill one drop into the conjunctival sac of the affected eye
Avoid touching the dropper tip to the eye or any surface to prevent contamination
If used longer than 10 days, monitor intraocular pressure
moa: Corticosteroids inhibit the inflammatory response by inducing phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins (lipocortins), which reduce release of arachidonic acid and thus the synthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes. They suppress edema, fibrin deposition, capillary dilation and proliferation, leukocyte migration, fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition, and scar formation; they may also delay healing. Difluprednate is deacetylated in vivo to the active metabolite 6alpha,9-difluoroprednisolone 17-butyrate (DFB).

absolute: Most active viral diseases of the cornea and conjunctiva including epithelial herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic keratitis), vaccinia, and varicella
monitor: Intraocular pressure (especially beyond 10 days of use)
Lens for posterior subcapsular cataract on prolonged use

preg: Animal studies showed embryotoxic and teratogenic effects after systemic administration, but topical ocular use produces minimal systemic absorption (blood levels below quantification limits); use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether topical ophthalmic corticosteroids reach detectable levels in breast milk; systemically administered corticosteroids appear in milk. Because systemic absorption from ophthalmic use is minimal, exercise caution when used in a nursing woman.
renal: Systemic absorption is negligible; no renal dose adjustment is needed.
hepatic: Systemic absorption is negligible; no hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

moderate: Other ophthalmic corticosteroids or NSAIDs may compound effects on healing
interactions.diagnostics: Prolonged use may raise intraocular pressure; monitor IOP.

serious: Corneal or scleral thinning with risk of perforation

counsel: Use exactly as directed and complete the tapering schedule; do not stop abruptly
Do not let the dropper tip touch your eye or any surface
Remove contact lenses before use and follow your doctor's advice on reinserting them
Report eye pain, worsening redness, vision changes, or discharge promptly
Long-term use requires eye-pressure checks; keep your follow-up appointments
pk: Local anti-inflammatory effect within days of regular dosing
Local ocular effect; systemic levels below quantification (50 ng/mL)
Effect maintained with regular dosing; taper to discontinue
Store at 15-25 C (59-77 F); do not freeze; keep tightly closed
pearls: Class risks: steroid-induced IOP rise, cataract, infection, and delayed healing
Contraindicated in active herpetic, mycobacterial, and fungal eye disease
Check IOP if used beyond 10 days
missed: Instill the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up.
overdose: Acute overdose is unlikely with ophthalmic use; accidental excess instillation can be flushed from the eye with warm tap water. Prolonged or excessive use may cause systemic corticosteroid effects and local complications such as raised intraocular pressure.
